content: There are minor differences in the oral absorption, bioavailability, and tolerability of different artemisinin derivatives. However, there is no evidence to suggest that these differences are clinically significant in the currently available formulations. The efficacy of a formulation is primarily determined by the properties of the partner medicine and the level of resistance to it. Policy-makers should consider the following factors when selecting antimalarial combination therapies (ACTs): Local data on the therapeutic efficacy of the ACT. Local data on drug resistance patterns. The adverse effect profiles of the ACT partner drugs. The availability of appropriate formulations to ensure patient adherence. Cost considerations. In parts of Southeast Asia, resistance to artemisinin is undermining the efficacy of ACTs and increasing the selection pressure on partner medicines. In other regions, there is no convincing evidence of reduced susceptibility to artemisinins. Therefore, the performance of the partner drugs becomes the key determinant in the choice of ACTs. Resistance to mefloquine has been observed in parts of mainland Southeast Asia where the drug has been heavily used. Despite this, the combination of artesunate and mefloquine remains highly effective unless resistance to artemisinin is also present. Resistance to both components has compromised the efficacy of artesunate + mefloquine in western Cambodia, eastern Myanmar, and eastern Thailand. Lumefantrine shares some cross-resistance with mefloquine, but this has not affected its efficacy in areas where artemether + lumefantrine has been used outside Southeast Asia. Until recently, there was no evidence of resistance to piperaquine, but reduced susceptibility has now been reported in western Cambodia. Elsewhere, the combination of dihydroartemisinin + piperaquine remains highly effective. Resistance to sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine (SP) limits its use in combination with artesunate to areas where susceptibility is retained. Amodiaquine remains effective in combination with artesunate in parts of Africa and the Americas, although resistance to this drug was prevalent in some areas before its introduction in ACTs. Artemisinin derivatives (e.g., artesunate, artemether, dihydroartemisinin) should not be used as monotherapy. To simplify use, improve adherence, and minimize the availability of oral artemisinin monotherapy, fixed-dose combination ACTs are strongly preferred over co-blistered or co-dispensed loose tablets. Fixed-dose combinations of all recommended ACTs are now available, except for artesunate + SP. Fixed-dose artesunate + amodiaquine performs better than loose tablets, likely due to ensuring adequate dosing. Unfortunately, pediatric formulations are not yet available for all ACTs. The choice of ACT in a country or region should be based on optimal efficacy and adherence, which can be achieved by: Minimizing the number of formulations available for each recommended treatment regimen. Using solid formulations instead of liquid formulations, even for young patients, where available. Although there are minor differences in the oral absorption and bioavailability of different artemisinin derivatives, there is no evidence that these differences in currently available formulations are clinically significant. The pharmacokinetic properties of the partner medicine and the level of resistance to it largely determine the efficacy and choice of combinations. Outside Southeast Asia, there is no convincing evidence yet for reduced susceptibility to artemisinins. Therefore, the performance of the partner drug is the main determinant in the choice of ACTs, according to the following principles: Drugs used in intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy (IPTp), seasonal malaria chemoprevention (SMC), or chemoprophylaxis should not be used as first-line treatment in the same country or region. In most malaria-endemic countries, first-line ACTs remain highly effective, although resistance patterns change over time and should be closely monitored. The use of fixed-dose combination formulations ensures strict adherence to the central principle of combination therapy. Monotherapies should not be used, except as parenteral therapy for severe malaria or SP chemoprevention. Steps should be taken to reduce and remove their market availability. Fixed-dose combination formulations are now available for all recommended ACTs except artesunate + SP. Pediatric formulations should allow accurate dosing without breaking tablets and should promote adherence by being acceptable to children. Pediatric formulations are currently available for artemether + lumefantrine, dihydroartemisinin + piperaquine, and artesunate + mefloquine. To optimize the benefits of deploying ACTs, they should be available in the public health delivery system, the private sector, and the community, with no financial or physical barriers to access. A strategy for ensuring full access (including community management of malaria in the context of integrated case management) must be based on analyses of national and local health systems and may require legislative changes and regulatory approval, with additional local adjustments as indicated by program monitoring and operational research. Community case management of malaria is recommended by WHO to improve access to prompt, effective treatment of malaria episodes by trained community members living as close as possible to the patients. The use of ACTs in this context is feasible, acceptable, and effective. Pre-referral treatment for severe malaria with rectal artesunate and the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) are also recommended in this context. Community case management should be integrated into community management of childhood illnesses, ensuring coverage of priority childhood illnesses outside of health facilities. Health education is vital to optimizing antimalarial treatment. Clear guidelines in the language understood by local users, posters, wall charts, educational videos, and other teaching materials, public awareness campaigns, and the provision of information materials to shopkeepers and other dispensers can improve the understanding of malaria. These efforts will increase the likelihood of better prescribing and adherence, appropriate referral, and reduced unnecessary use of antimalarial medicines. Patient adherence is a major determinant of the response to antimalarial drugs, as most treatments are taken at home without medical supervision. Studies on adherence suggest that 3-day regimens of medicines such as ACTs are completed reasonably well, provided that patients or caregivers are given an adequate explanation at the time of prescribing or dispensing. Prescribers, shopkeepers, and vendors should therefore give clear, comprehensible explanations of how to use the medicines. Co-formulation likely contributes significantly to adherence. Blister packs also encourage the completion of a treatment course and correct dosing. Pharmacovigilance, the practice of monitoring the effects of medical drugs after they have been licensed for use, is essential to identify and evaluate previously unreported adverse reactions. A practical handbook on the pharmacovigilance of antimalarial medicines provides a step-by-step approach for antimalarial pharmacovigilance, focusing on active and passive pharmacovigilance, reporting, event monitoring, and other key factors. In the final phase of malaria elimination and prevention of re-establishment, WHO recommends that all countries ensure access to malaria prevention, diagnosis, and treatment as part of universal health coverage. Countries or areas that have attained very low to low levels of transmission require additional interventions to eliminate malaria. These strategies may include mass drug administration (MDA), mass relapse prevention (MRP), or mass testing and treatment (MTaT). However, mass strategies are generally not recommended for post-elimination settings unless there is a resumption of local transmission of malaria. Mass testing and treatment (MTaT) involves parasitological testing of the entire population of a delimited geographical area and treatment of all positive cases with an appropriate antimalarial medicine at approximately the same time. MTaT is an active case detection strategy that may improve the timeliness and coverage of treatment. However, MTaT does not provide a population-level prophylactic period as MDA does. Providing antimalarial medicine only to those who are known to be infected may improve adherence to treatment, population acceptance of the intervention, and equity while decreasing the risk of unintended consequences. In post-elimination settings, malaria programs must continue to actively intervene to prevent the re-establishment of transmission. Countries will need to ensure that diagnosis and treatment services are available everywhere as part of universal health coverage, as imported cases can be identified anywhere and at any time. The extent and intensity of additional activities during the post-elimination period will depend on the health system and the malariogenic potential of the area, including the degree of receptivity to transmission and the risk or rate of importation of malaria infections.
